title: Sliding Window Median
description: Compute the median of every sliding window, maintaining an always-sorted window with binary-search insertion and removal.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and a window size k, return the median of every contiguous window of size k as it slides from the start to the end of the array. For an odd-sized window, the median is the single middle value; for an even-sized window, it is the average of the two middle values.

blocks.caption: Keeping the window sorted lets both insertion, removal, and median lookup avoid a full re-sort.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] (can contain duplicates and negatives), k (window size)"],["Output","One median value per window, in order, as the window slides right by one each time"],["Median rule","Odd k: the single middle sorted value. Even k: average of the two middle sorted values"]]}

blocks.text: A sliding window that needs the MEDIAN (not just a sum or count) at every position needs the window's contents in SORTED order to answer quickly. Since only one element enters and one leaves per step, maintaining a sorted structure incrementally (rather than re-sorting the whole window every time) is the key optimization.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This extends the sliding window family (Sliding Window Maximum, Maximum Number of Robots Within Budget) to a query that a simple running aggregate or monotonic deque cannot answer directly, since the median depends on the full sorted order, not just the extreme values.

Picture a shelf of books kept sorted by height, representing the current window. As the window slides, one book (the newest element) slides onto the shelf in its correct sorted position, and another book (the oldest element leaving the window) is removed from wherever it sits. The book (or pair of books) exactly in the middle of the shelf is always the median.

blocks.caption: Binary search finds the exact sorted slot for both insertion and removal.

items: Keeping the window sorted at all times means the median is always readable directly from the middle index (or two middle indices), in O(1).
Binary search finds the correct insertion position for a new element, and the exact position of the element leaving the window, in O(log k) each.
Actually inserting into or removing from a sorted ARRAY still costs O(k) to shift elements, but this avoids the more expensive full re-sort of the whole window on every step.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The medians produced are [1, -1, -1, 3, 5, 6], matching the expected output exactly. Since k = 3 is odd, every median is simply the middle element of the 3-element sorted window.

The most direct approach re-sorts the entire window from scratch at every position, which correctly gives the median but repeats a lot of work, since most of the window is unchanged between consecutive positions.

Since only one element changes at a time, maintaining the window as an always-sorted array lets binary search locate both the new element's insertion point and the departing element's position in O(log k), rather than paying for a full O(k log k) re-sort every step.
Re-sort each window from scratch and read off the median directly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n * k log k)","Each of the n-k+1 windows is sorted from scratch"],["Space","O(k)","The temporary window copy per position"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Re-sorting the whole window ignores that only one element changes per step; the sorted order of the other k-1 elements is already known from the previous window.

Maintain the window as an always-sorted array. On each slide, binary search for the insertion position of the entering element and insert it there, then binary search for the exact position of the departing element and remove it. Read the median directly from the middle index (or average the two middle indices for even k).

items: Initialize the sorted window once from the first k elements, O(k log k).
Each subsequent step: binary search insert (O(log k) search, O(k) shift) and binary search remove (O(log k) search, O(k) shift).
Median lookup is O(1), reading the middle index or indices directly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, re-sort each window","O(n * k log k)","O(k)"],["Optimized, sorted array with binary search insert/remove","O(n * k)","O(k)"]]}

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: A balanced BST or two-heap structure can push this further to O(n log k), but the sorted-array-with-binary-search approach is simpler to implement correctly and already removes the log k re-sort factor from every window.

items: A sliding window query needing full sorted order (like the median) cannot be answered by a simple running sum or monotonic deque; it needs an actual maintained sorted structure.
Since only one element enters and one leaves per step, incrementally updating a sorted structure avoids the cost of a full re-sort.
Binary search finds the correct position for both insertion and removal in a sorted array, even though the array shift itself remains O(k).

blocks.text: Sliding Window Median is solved by maintaining the current window as an always-sorted array, using binary search to find the correct insertion and removal positions as the window slides, and reading the median directly from the middle of the sorted array. This avoids re-sorting the whole window at every step, reducing the total work from O(n * k log k) to O(n * k).
